core.text: A describing word like *magnus* (big) or *bonus* (good) has no shape of its own: it copies the noun it goes with. That copying is **an adjective agreeing with its noun (same gender, number and case)**, *adiectīvum cum substantīvō congruēns*. Ørberg lists an adjective as *magnus -a -um*: three shapes, one per gender, each declining like the matching noun. The adjective may stand before or after its noun.
English adjectives never change: *big river*, *big rivers*, *big island*. Latin's do, and the change is how you know which noun an adjective belongs to when the two are far apart.
Find the noun's gender, number and case and give the adjective the same three. The endings often rhyme (*puella bona*) but need not (*vir bonus*, *puer bonus*).

invented.en: The good shepherd sees the small sheep.

core.text: *Puer* (boy) has no -us and *ovis* (sheep) no -a, yet *puer bonus* and *ovis parva* are right: agreement copies the noun's gender, not its letters. Ask what the noun is (masculine, feminine or neuter), then pick the adjective's form; never just match the sound of the ending.

teach.title: What agreeing means
teach.say: A describing word has no shape of its own. It is an adjective agreeing with its noun (same gender, number and case): it takes all three from the noun it belongs to. Ørberg prints it *magnus -a -um*, one word with three tails. In *Sicilia īnsula magna … est*, *magna* wears -a because *īnsula* is feminine and single. English has one *big* for an island and for rivers alike, so in Latin the tail, not the place in the line, tells you which noun an adjective belongs to, and it may stand before or after that noun. These steps teach two of the three matches, gender and number. The third, case, is what makes *in prōvinciā Rōmānā* and *in capitulō prīmō* change both words together after *in*; it is taught with the cases themselves, so here you need only notice that the two tails move as a pair.

teach.title: With a feminine noun: -a
teach.say: *Prōvincia* is feminine and single, so its adjective ends -a: *prōvincia Rōmāna*. With a-nouns the two tails happen to rhyme, which makes this the easiest pair to hear.

teach.title: With a masculine noun: -us
teach.say: *Numerus* is masculine and single, so the adjective ends -us: *numerus secundus*. Same word as *secunda*, different tail.

teach.title: With a neuter noun: -um
teach.say: *Oppidum* is neuter and single, so the adjective ends -um: *oppidum Rōmānum*. Three genders, three tails — -us, -a, -um, the order the dictionary prints them in.

teach.title: More than one: -ī, -ae, -a
teach.say: In the plural the three tails become -ī for masculine, -ae for feminine and -a for neuter: *fluviī magnī*, *īnsulae parvae*, *oppida Rōmāna*. The adjective follows its noun into the plural as readily as it follows its gender.

teach.title: Copy the gender, not the letters
teach.say: *Aegyptus* ends in -us, but it is feminine, because the names of countries are: so a describing word on *Aegyptus* is feminine too — *Magna est Aegyptus*, never *magnus*. Ask what the noun’s gender is and then choose the tail; never match the sound of the ending.

more.text: From the learner's notes (weeks 1 and 3): an adjective takes on the gender of its noun, then its number, and — once the accusative (the object form) is learned — its case as well. Because -us -a -um adjectives use the us-noun, a-noun and um-noun endings, there are no new forms to learn: accusative -um / -am / -um, plural -ōs / -ās / -a. Where the noun has a different pattern the endings stop rhyming: *propheta malus*, *domus mala*, *pānēs bonī*, *carnēs bonae*.

Adjectives in -er drop the e in the other forms (*pulcher, pulchra, pulchrum*; *niger, nigra, nigrum*) though a few keep it (*miser, misera*). An adjective after *est* agrees with the subject (*Iūlia laeta est*). Used alone, an adjective becomes a noun: *multī* = many people, *pauca* = few things; and *mālum* (apple, long a) is a different word from *malum* (a bad thing). Adjectives of the third declension (*fortis*, *brevis*) come later. Ørberg cap. I–V; A&G §286.
